chunks.text:
from Peanuts
Hi Chi,
Last year I wrote about Formula 1 and late-night texts, about finding each other again through the dumbest possible things: reels at 2am, memes that weren’t even that funny. This year we got closer in the way that actually changes something.
The first half of 2025, we had real conversations: the kind of talking where you say something you haven’t fully articulated before and watch it become clearer as you speak. There’s a difference between “we know each other” and “we can actually talk,” and we crossed that line somewhere in the spring. I noticed because the texture of our messages changed, less performative, more porous. You started telling me things before you’d figured out what they meant. That’s trust.
And then you found M. I watched it happen from the periphery of your stories. Your messages got lighter, then less frequent in that particular way that means someone else is holding the other end of the thread now. The silences were presence, just pointed somewhere else. I recognized the shape of it. I was happy.

Fromm has this way of cutting through the romantic fog. Love, he says, is a practice (care, responsibility, respect, knowledge) sustained over time, through the parts that aren’t easy:1
Love is an activity, not a passive affect; it is a "standing in," not a "falling for."Erich Fromm, The Art of Loving (1956)
I think that’s why watching you fall into something stable felt so right. It was you choosing and being chosen, over and over, in the small moments that don’t make it into the story but constitute the actual relationship. The willingness to stay when staying is boring.
If the love is the Fromm kind, the active kind, you become a denser version of yourself, and that density leaks outward into everything else. That’s what I see happening with you. You’re becoming more visible. The love is making you realer.

I’m glad that you found your person this year. I’m glad that we had the conversations earlier this year, the crossing-over from acquaintance-friendship into something that can hold weight. I want it to survive the calendar shift, the relationship shift, whatever new life you’re growing into. I’m not trying to compete with it. I’m cheering for all of it.
Last year I quoted Simone Weil: ”attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.”2 We paid attention to each other through the dumb things. This year the attention got quieter, more serious. I’m grateful you found someone who pays attention the way you deserve. And I’m still here, still watching the cars go in circles.

remarque


erich fromm, the art of loving (1956), especially chapters 1–2. the core argument: love is an art that requires knowledge and effort. the four elements he names are care, responsibility, respect and knowledge. ↩


simone weil, letter to joë bousquet, 13 april 1942. ↩
